segments.title: The scenario and the order
sections: The Stop That Was Chosen Last

cues.text: The level was on your sheet, the plan you mark before the session. The trigger fired, the bar close that says enter now. You clicked in with the size you always use.
Then you looked for a stop. Behind the zone, the band of prices around a level, was too far for that size.
So the stop went a few points under your entry, inside the zone, where the loss felt bearable.
Two bars later it was gone, and price went on to the target without you.
Or the stop held, but the target was a level eleven points away, so the winner paid less than the loser cost.
The stop was chosen last and tested first. That is not a plan. That is a coin flip with extra steps.
Now, the order. Every trade here follows one chain: idea, setup, trigger, construction.
Construction is the last link: the arithmetic that turns three answered questions into an order.
One: the target, a level you are heading toward.
Two: the stop, behind the far edge of the zone.
Three: the risk, and the 2 to 1 check.
Four: the size.
Five: the entry.
Now, the target. It comes first: the one number that decides whether the rest is worth doing.
A target is a level from your list, written before the session on the branch, your if-then line for that level. It says where price may travel. It is never a reason to enter.
On this composite chart, invented prices, a long at the prior-day-high zone targets prior-week-high, a zone from 24,223.00 to 24,230.00.
Price coming up reaches the bottom first. That bottom is the near edge, so the target price is 24,223.00.
Not a target: take 2R.
Not a target: twenty handles, which means points.
Not a target: a round number.
Not a target: an indicator, or new highs. None of these is a place where anything has happened before.
The rule: the target is a level from your list, written on the branch before the session, and its price is the near edge of that zone.
Getting it wrong is an entry with no target, managed by watching the open profit. The exit then belongs to your nerves, not the chart.
The fix: the target line holds a level slug, the short name you log it under, and a price. R or points: struck out, no trade.

segments.title: The stop and the 2 to 1 filter
sections: The Stop Goes Behind The Far Edge

cues.text: The stop is where the trade is wrong: price has gone through the whole zone it was built on.
So the stop sits behind the far edge, the side of the zone away from where price arrives. Above price, the top. Below, the bottom.
It also clears the trigger's extreme: for a Pause N Go long, where price holds in the zone, then goes, below the pause low.
How far behind, you write once on your PlayBook page, your own book of rules. These examples use 2 points.
A stop of always twenty ticks never looked at the chart. Consistent, like a stopped clock.
Now, the stop floor: the smallest stop a page of yours accepts, from your own record of how far trades run against you.
The far edge comes first. If the floor is wider, the stop goes out to it, and the size falls.
No indicator places a stop, ATR, the average true range, included.
The rule: the stop goes behind the far edge and the trigger extreme by your written distance, or out to your floor if wider, resting at the broker from entry.
Getting it wrong is a stop inside the zone, to allow more contracts. The size came first, and the stop moved to fit.
The fix: write the far edge and the stop as a pair before the session. The order matches that line.
Now, risk and the 2 to 1 filter. Risk runs from your intended price, the price the trigger says you enter at, to the stop.
The filter is one division: room to the target over distance to the stop. It must be 2 or more.
The example. Enter at 24,187.00 with the stop at 24,175.00. Risk is 12 points, 48 ticks.
The target, 24,223.00, is 36 points away. 36 over 12 is 3. That clears.
Had the target been 24,205.00, the room is 18 points: 1.5 to 1. No trade, however clean the trigger.
2R is a filter, not a target. A close target is no reason to tighten the stop. It is simply too close.
The rule: if the target is less than twice the risk away, there is no trade.
Getting it wrong is a 1.3 to 1 trade taken because the setup looked perfect. You are pricing it by how sure you feel.
The fix: write room over risk on every order. Under 2, the next word you write is no.

segments.title: Base R and the size
sections: Base R Is Fixed Before Any Trade
Size Comes From The Stop And The Grade

cues.text: Base R is the one number here that comes from you, not the chart: the fixed amount you risk on a full-size trade. Every result is measured in it.
You choose it once, in three written lines.
One: the run of full losses in a row you can take without changing anything.
Two: the kill-switch days in a row you can take. The kill switch is the daily limit, 2R, twice base R.
Three: the amount at which the larger of those totals is a loss your account survives, and you still trade your next session as written.
Write it, dated, on the first page of your PlayBook.
The rule: base R is one number, written and dated, the same on every trade, changed only at a scheduled review.
Getting it wrong is a bigger R after three green days, or a smaller one after a kill-switch day. A risk number that follows your mood is not a risk number. It is a mood ring.
The fix: the size line starts with base R, from page one. Any other first number is not a size line.
Now, size. One division: base R over the stop value per contract, rounded down.
On MNQ, the micro Nasdaq contract, a tick is 0.25 points, worth 0.50. 48 ticks is 24.
Say base R is 100, chosen because it divides easily, not a recommendation. 100 over 24 is 4.17, so 4 contracts.
Always down: rounding up is a silent rise in risk. Zero contracts is no trade.
Now, the grade: the score an entry gets before it resolves, from four checks. It sets the R in that sum.
One: the location is a named level.
Two: the trigger fired before entry.
Three: the stop is behind structure.
Four: the size matches the plan for that stop.
The table: A plus and A trade base R, B half, C no trade. A plus adds a fill within 2 ticks.
Conviction, the branch's strength count from Module 09, never changes size. Nor does the day so far, or the feeling that this one is different.
The rule: size is the grade share of base R over the stop value per contract, rounded down, with the arithmetic written.
Getting it wrong is the same three contracts on every trade, whatever the stop. The size came before the structure was read.
The fix: write the sum before the order goes.

sections: The Exits Are Written Before The Entry
The Stop You Want To Move

cues.text: The fifth line is the entry: the order, its intended price written first, so the fill can be measured.
Every exit is decided before that order goes. There are three.
One: the target.
Two: the stop, behind the far edge.
Three: one planned scale. Half comes off at 2R. The other half is the runner, held to the target.
The example. The long from before: entry 24,187.00, four contracts, risk 12 points.
2R is 24 points, so the scale is two contracts at 24,211.00, and the runner two contracts to 24,223.00.
The stop at 24,175.00 covers all four. All three orders go with the entry. Your nerves are not on the ticket.
Moving a working target, in or out, is a Fail on the execution mark, the Pass or Fail written after the exit.
Automatic breakeven is off. A stop moved to entry after the scale is outside the plan: Too Early, the journal tag for it.
The rule: the target, the one planned scale and the stop are written and sent with the entry. Nothing else.
Getting it wrong is an entry sent alone, stop and target to follow. The plan is in your head, so the last three bars rewrite it.
The fix: a bracket template that sends stop, scale and target together, breakeven and trail off.

cues.chapter: The stop you want to move
cues.text: Now, the stop you want to move. Once the trade is on, the arithmetic is done and the hard part starts.
Price nears your stop and you want to give it room. Or it runs your way and you want to protect it.
Same urge: a decision made with a position on, replacing one made clear-headed.
Widening the stop is Broke Rule, the tag for a broken hard rule, every time. It raises risk above the size.
Tightening is Too Early, except a move to an invalidation, the close that proves the idea wrong, written on the entry line with its price.
A price you find after entry, like a new swing low, is not that exception.
The rule: once the order is sent, the stop is never widened, and tightened only to an invalidation written at entry.
Getting it wrong is dragging the stop behind each new bar. The risk is reset by feel, so the grade at entry describes a trade that no longer exists.
The fix: after the bracket, write one line: stop, scale, target, invalidation. Read it before you touch an order.

cues.text: Two composite cases, invented prices, each stopping once the orders work.
The branch, written at 9:10 a.m. The zone is pd-high, the prior-day high, 24,177.00 to 24,186.00.
If price accepts above it, a 5-minute close beyond the zone, and a Pause N Go fires on the pullback, then prior-week-high, near edge 24,223.00.
The pre-open check: 9 points of zone plus 2 behind, so an entry at the near edge risks 11. Twice that is 22. The target is 37 above the zone. The branch stays.
The setup and the trigger. At 9:58 a.m. price touches the zone, and a 5-minute bar closes at 24,191.50, accepted above. It pulls back.

cues.text: Take your last ten trades. Score each a point for every one of six lines that is true.
One, target. A level with its price, written before entry.
Two, stop. Behind the far edge by your written distance, or at your floor if that was wider.
Three, ratio. Room divided by risk at the intended price, and 2 or more.
Four, size. The table share of base R over the stop value, rounded down, arithmetic written.
Five, entry. The intended price written, and the stop, scale and target sent with the order.
Six, hands off. After entry, nothing moved except the planned scale and an invalidation written at entry.
The rule: a constructed trade scores six out of six. A miss on line two or four breached a grade check: a C, which is no trade.
A miss on line three should not have been sent. A miss on line six carries Too Early or Broke Rule.
Now, reading it. If three or more of the ten scored under six, find the line you missed most often and fix it before your next order.
Getting it wrong is scoring from memory. Memory is a generous marker, and everyone gets six out of six. Read the lines off the journal, the note and the ticket.
Your assignment. On your next trade, write the five construction lines in order before the order goes: target, stop, risk with its ratio, size with its arithmetic, entry.
If the ratio line is under 2, the fifth line reads no trade. That is the whole assignment.
In one line: the target level, the stop behind the far edge, the risk and the 2 to 1 check, the size from base R and the grade, then the entry with its exits written.
A wider stop changes the size, never the risk. A target too close for 2 to 1 is no trade.
Where it goes next. Module 15, Writing The Plan, puts the first line of construction on paper before the session: every branch names its zone and its target.
Module 16, The Pre-Market Routine, carries those lines onto the sheet by 9:25 a.m., and Module 17 is where the bracket is sent, then left alone.
In the journal, Module 18, the grade is written at entry from the four checks, and the intended price sits beside the fill.
Your base R and your stop floor live in your PlayBook, Module 23.

check.q: A trade missing line two or four was…
options: A C, which is no trade
Fine if the next trade is better
check.why: Those lines are the third and fourth grade checks: a stop behind structure and a size that matches the plan.

check.q: A trade missing line three, the ratio, should…
check.why: Under 2 to 1 is no trade, however clean the trigger.

check.q: Scoring your ten trades from memory…
options: Is fine for the oldest trades
Scores everything high: read the lines off the journal
check.why: The lines are read off the journal, the note and the ticket, never off recall.

check.q: The assignment: if the ratio line is under 2, the entry line reads…
check.why: The fifth line reads no trade, and the order is not sent.

options: Target, stop, risk and the 2 to 1 check, size, entry
questions.why: The target comes first, the entry last with its exits already written.

questions.q: For a long arriving at a zone from below, the target price is…
options: The far edge of the zone
The near edge, the side price reaches first
questions.why: The target is a level from your list, and its price is the near edge of that zone.

questions.q: The stop floor means the stop goes…
options: Behind the far edge, or out to the floor if the floor is wider
questions.why: The far edge first, then the floor if it is wider. A wider stop cuts the size, never raises the risk.

questions.q: Entry 24,100.00, stop 24,090.00, target 24,118.00. The trade is…
questions.why: Room 18 divided by risk 10 is 1.8, under 2. Size and a tighter stop inside the zone do not repair it.

questions.q: Base R 100, a 30-tick stop at 0.50 per tick per contract, an A grade. Contracts:
questions.why: 30 ticks is 15 per contract. 100 divided by 15 is 6.67, rounded down to 6.
A plus and A trade base R, B trades half, C is no trade.

questions.q: Besides the target and the stop, the one exit planned before entry is…
options: One planned scale: half off at 2R
questions.why: Everything else is a new decision made with a position on.

questions.q: After entry you move the stop to a new swing low. That is…
options: Too Early if tightened, Broke Rule if widened
questions.why: Only an invalidation written on the entry line is allowed, and a price found after entry is not one.
